title: Portosystemic anastomoses in portal hypertension
claims: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein; the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein.
The portal vein supplies about 75% of the liver's blood flow; blood leaves the liver through the hepatic veins into the IVC.
Portal hypertension is a hepatic venous pressure gradient above 5 mmHg; it becomes clinically significant at 10 mmHg, and varices can bleed above 12 mmHg. Cirrhosis is the most common cause.
Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals and causes splenomegaly (often with thrombocytopenia) and ascites.
Oesophageal varices: left gastric (coronary) vein (portal) → oesophageal veins → azygos vein (systemic).
Acute variceal bleeding: resuscitation, IV octreotide, IV antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. ceftriaxone), and endoscopic band ligation within 12 hours.
Primary prevention of variceal bleeding: a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol, nadolol or carvedilol) or endoscopic band ligation.
Caput medusae: paraumbilical veins (portal, in the ligamentum teres) → superficial and inferior epigastric veins (systemic) around the umbilicus.
In caput medusae from portal hypertension, flow in the periumbilical veins runs away from the umbilicus.
Anorectal varices: superior rectal vein (portal, via the inferior mesenteric vein) → middle rectal (to internal iliac) and inferior rectal (to internal pudendal) veins (systemic).
Anorectal varices are distinct from haemorrhoids; haemorrhoids are not more common in portal hypertension.
TIPS places a stent through the liver from a hepatic vein (usually the right) to a portal vein branch, creating a low-resistance portosystemic shunt.
TIPS indications: variceal bleeding refractory to endoscopic and drug therapy, and refractory ascites. Main complication: hepatic encephalopathy.
